en: *The Treatise on the Eighteen Schools*, one fascicle;
translated by Paramārtha of the Chen dynasty.
15. *The Section on the Analysis of Parts*, from the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, Fascicle Lower; Section Fifteen: The Analysis of Parts.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa..."
Regarding future disciples,
how are the various divisions distinguished?
What constitutes the root?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"In the future, my disciples shall consist of twenty schools."
It enables all dharmas to abide in the world.
Those belonging to this school have all attained the four fruits of the śramaṇa.
The Tripiṭaka is impartial, being without inferior, middling, or superior grades.
For example, the taste of the ocean water is without variation.
It is as if a person has twenty sons;
this is what the Tathāgata has truly taught.
Mañjuśrī, the two fundamental divisions emerge from the Mahāyāna;
from the Prajñāpāramitā emerge the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
All Buddhas emerge from the Prajñāpāramitā.
Mañjuśrī, it is like earth, water, fire, wind, and space.
This is the dwelling place of all sentient beings.
Likewise, this Prajñāpāramitā and the Mahāyāna are the source from which all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas emerge.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
what is meant by 'sections'?"
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"Regarding the first two schools:
the first is the Mahāsāṃghika, which means 'the Great Assembly'—it refers to the Vinaya collection where elders and juniors gather together in a single assembly."
The two bodies, *Vibhajya*—this term refers to the elders (*sthavira*). It is only the elders who, having assembled together, produced the Vinaya-piṭaka.
One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, these two schools shall arise.
Later, the Mahāsāṃghika produced seven schools.
Within these one hundred years, one school emerged called Ekavyāvahārika; it is called "One" because its tenets were identical to those of the Mahāsāṃghika.
Within one hundred years, from the Lokāyatika school,
another school emerged named Lokottaravāda, which is a term of praise meaning "transcending the world.
Within those same one hundred years, from the Lokottaravāda...
One school emerged, named the Kaukkuṭika; this was derived from the clan name of the Vinaya master.
Within one hundred years, this school arose from the Kaukkuṭika.
The name Bahusrutiya signifies that the founder of this school possessed the wisdom of extensive learning (*bahuśruta*).
Within a hundred years, a sect emerged from the Bahusrutīyas called Caityaśaila; this mountain was the residence of the founder of that school.
Within one hundred years, a school emerged from the Cetiya [Vihāra],
named the Pūrvaśaila (East Mountain), which was also the dwelling place of its founder.
Within another hundred years, a school emerged from the Pūrvaśaila.
It is called the Northern Mountain (Uttarāpatha), which was also the residence of the Master of the Vinaya.
This refers to how [the schools] emerged from the Mahāsāṃghika school into seven schools, including the original Mahāsāṃghika itself.
These constitute the eight schools.
Within a hundred years, from the Tāmraśātīya school,
eleven schools emerged.

Within the first hundred years, one school emerged named Sarvāstivāda (The Proponents of the Existence of All). It is called "all that is spoken" because its masters maintain that all three time periods exist.
Within those hundred years...
From all languages, one school emerged,
named Haimavata (Snowy Mountain), which was also the practice of the Vinaya masters.
Within a hundred years, from the Snowy Mountain, one school emerged.
Vatsīputra was the clan name of the founder of this Vinaya school;
within one hundred years, a single sect emerged from the Vātsīputrīyas.
Dharmottara is the name of the Vinaya Master;
within a hundred years, a school emerged from Dharmottara named Bhadrayānīya,
which is the name of the Vinaya Master Bhadra.
Within one hundred years, from the Bhadrayānīya school, there emerged a sub-sect named Sarvāstivāda;
its masters of the Vinaya were esteemed by all and honored by the learned.
Within another hundred years, from the Sarvāstivāda, there emerged a sub-sect.
This is the dwelling place of the Vinaya Master Śaivala.
Within the hundred-year period, a school emerged from Mount Śaivala known as the Mahā-avaivartika (Great Non-Abandonment).
Regarding its founder, when the Vinaya Master was first born, his mother abandoned him in a well.
The father pursued him;
although he fell, he did not perish prematurely.
Therefore, it is said that he was not abandoned.
It is also called Nengshe (Capable of Shooting).
Within one hundred years, a school emerged from the Mahāsaṃghika known as the Dharmaguptaka;
"Dharmagupta" is the name of its founder.
Within the first hundred years, a school emerged from the Dharmaguptaka;
its founder was named Kāśyapīya, which was his clan name.
Within the [same] hundred years, a school emerged from the Kāśyapīya.
The term *sūtra-pada* refers to the meaning of the *sūtra* as upheld by the masters of the Vinaya;
this means that when the *tattvavādin* school includes the eleven divisions,
and when the *tattvavādin* establishes twelve divisions.
The Buddha spoke these verses.
According to the Mahāsāṃghika school, there are seven distinct bodies of the Vibhajyavādins and eleven others; these are called the twenty schools.
The eighteen schools and the two original ones All emerge from the Mahāyāna;
There is neither "is" nor "is not. I declare they will arise in the future.
Compiled by Dharma Master Kumārajīva After the Parinirvāṇa of the Perfectly Awakened One.
When more than a hundred years had passed, divergent doctrines arose here;
the True Dharma gradually declined and vanished.
Each person gave rise to different views and established separate assemblies—how perilous and truly fearsome!
One should give rise to a mind of weary detachment; now,
examining the Buddha’s true teaching within the sūtras,
one relies on the ultimate truth to seek its firm meaning, just as one might seek gold among sand and pebbles.
Having obtained the treasure of true gold,
I heard from a former victor that one hundred and sixteen years after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, the Buddha among men,
there was a city named Pāṭaliputra.
At that time, King Aśoka reigned over Jambudvīpa and governed the world. During that period,
the Great Sangha was divided into separate schools with differing doctrines.
At that time, there were two bhikṣus:
the first was named Neng,
and the second was named Inyuan.
The third is called "much-hearing" (bahuśruta).
It is said that there are five points for teaching sentient beings, namely:
benefiting others, and [teaching] those who lack knowledge.
They doubted that the Way could be attained through the observation of conventional discourse;
these were the two schools from which the Buddha’s teaching first arose:
the first was called the Mahāsāṃghika.
The second refers to the Tāmraśāṭīya, which in the language of Qin is called the Sthavira school; within these same hundred-odd years,
the Mahāsāṃghika school further gave rise to other sub-sects.
First is called the Single Explanation;
second is called the Supramundane Explanation;
third is called Dwelling in Caves.
Furthermore, during more than one hundred years,
another sub-sect emerged within the Mahāsāṃghika school.
It is called the Prajñapti-śāstra.
Furthermore, during the second century,
the non-Buddhist renunciant Mahādeva went forth as a monk on Mount Caitya.
Within the Mahāsāṃghika school, three further sub-sects were established:
the first is named Caitīya,
and the second is named Bahuśrutīya.
The third was Uttarasela. Thus, within the Mahāsāṃghika school, it was divided into nine sections:
the first was named Mahāsāṃghika.
The second is called "Single Discourse.
The third is called "Supramundane Discourse.
The fourth is called "Cave-Dweller."
Fifth is named Bahuśruta;
sixth is named Prajñapti;
seventh is named Yugandhara.
The eighth is named Ārṣa;
the ninth is named Uttarīya-śaila school.
This lasted until the third century [after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa].
Within the Sthavira school, due to matters of dispute,
it was established as a separate sect;
one name is Sarvāstivāda.
The first was also called the Hetuvāda (Causalists), formerly known as the Sthavira-vāda;
the second was called the Haimavata (Himalayan School).
These occurred during this third century.
Within the Sarvāstivāda school, another sub-sect arose,
named the Vātsīputrīya;
this occurred during these three hundred years.
From the Vātsīputrīya school, two further sub-sects emerged:
the first was named Dharmottarīya,
and the second was named Bhadrayānīya.
The third is called Mili, also known as Sammitī;
the fourth is the Ṣaṭpārvatīya school.
Within these same three hundred years,
another sub-sect arose from within the Sarvāstivāda,
named the Mahīśāsaka.
From within the Mahīśāsaka school, another sub-sect arose;
because its founder and his tenets were associated with the name Dharmagupta,
it was established during this third century.
From within the Sarvāstivāda school,
another sub-sect arose,
named Ullūra, also known as Kāśyapīya.
Within four hundred years,
another distinct school arose within the Sarvāstivāda,
due to the Great Master Uttara.
It is called Saṃgītiparyāya,
and it is also called Sūtravibhaṅga.
Thus, within the Sthavira school...
It is divided into twelve schools: first, the Sthavira;
second, the Haimavata.
The third is called Sarvāstivāda;
the fourth, Vatsīputrīya;
and the fifth, Dharmottarīya.
Sixth is named Bhadrāyanī; seventh is named Miliṭi;
eighth is named Ṣaṭpurīya.
Ninth is the Mahīśāsaka;
tenth is the Dharmaguptaka;
eleventh is the Kāśyapīya.
The twelfth is the Sūtra-śāstra section.
I shall now explain its fundamental and intermediate meanings.
Regarding that Mahāsāṃghika school:
One teaching speaks of the supramundane, and another speaks of dwelling in caves;
these are all fundamentally taught as the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, being entirely supramundane.
There is no such thing as a Tathāgata that is a worldly phenomenon;
everything spoken by the Tathāgata is the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
It exhaustively explains all matters, all characteristics, and all meanings;
it declares that the Tathāgata’s form is boundless,
his radiance immeasurable, and his lifespan immeasurable.
He gives rise to mindfulness, faith, and joy without ever becoming weary;
the Buddha does not sleep,
and he provides answers without being questioned.
There is nothing to be spoken;
one should always unify the mind.
Sentient beings are neither manifold nor numerous.
All have heard and understood the teachings spoken by the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata knows all dharmas with a single mind;
through wisdom conjoined with a single thought-moment, he awakens to all dharmas.
At all times, until even his parinirvāṇa, the Tathāgata’s knowledge of exhaustion and knowledge of non-arising are constantly present before him.
The Bodhisattva does not crave the mother’s womb;
he descends into the mother’s womb in the form of a white elephant.
All Bodhisattvas are born from the right side.
The Bodhisattva is free from thoughts of attachment, anger, or malice;
yet for the sake of sentient beings, they vow to be born in the evil realms in order to bring all afflicted beings to maturity.
All that is heard, known, and perceived arises from the Noble Truths.
It is taught that there are the realms of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm,
which possess the six groups of consciousness.
The five sense-faculties are mere lumps of flesh;
the eye does not see forms, and so on,
until the body does not perceive tangibles.
Within meditative concentration, there is also verbal expression;
it also tames the mind and also sustains contemplation.
All conditioned phenomena have no fixed location.
The mental factors of a *srotāpanna* know themselves to be [on the path toward] an *arhat*.
There may be instances where they lack knowledge of the benefits conferred by others or harbor doubts.
By observing the speech of others, one attains the Way;
through wisdom and skillful means, one becomes detached from birth and death and also attains peace and happiness.
From the eighth [stage] down,
even the dharmas of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) are said to be subject to regression; this includes the regression of the *srotāpanna* from their dharma.
Arhats also possess the quality of falling away (parihāṇadharman).
They do not possess mundane right view,
but they do possess the mundane faculty of faith.
There are no indeterminate dharmas;
having transcended and emerged from the state of ordinary birth,
one does not sever all fetters at once.
A stream-enterer (srotāpanna) is capable of committing all manner of evil deeds,
with the sole exception of the crimes of immediate retribution (ānantarya).
All sūtras are based on the definitive meaning (nītārtha).
The nine kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are:
analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), space (*ākāśa*),

the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The twelve links of dependent origination, the factors of the path, and the nature of the mind are inherently pure.
The Buddha is defiled by adventitious afflictions;
the latent tendencies are not the mind itself, nor are they mental factors, as they lack an object-condition.
If the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) were distinct from the active fetters (*paryavasthāna*),
they would not be associated with the mind;
furthermore, there would be no past or future dharmas within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
It is not known by non-wisdom, nor is there a lack of remedy;
the Srotāpanna attains meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
Such as these are called the fundamental objects of vision.
Regarding those who hold intermediate views,
according to their specific observations,
there is little that is self-created.
There is little that is produced by another;
there is little arising from causes and conditions.
At one time, two minds may arise simultaneously.
The path is itself affliction and karma;
the seeds of perception are grasping;
and the transformation and continuity of the sense faculties and the four great elements constitute [the process].
It is neither mind nor mental factors.
The mind fills the body;
thus one can obtain and fully embrace such desires.
This is called what is seen in the intermediate stage.
Regarding the fundamental view of the learned,
the Buddha taught five kinds of supramundane dharmas.
The path leading to the cessation of suffering—impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and nirvana—is the supramundane;
all else is mundane.
An arhat may still derive benefit from others.
There are those who possess ignorance and doubt,
who attain the Way through the speech of others and through observation;
all other Sarvāstivādins hold views identical to these.
Regarding that fundamental view established by designation:
if one says that the aggregates (*skandhas*) are not karma,
then all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāras*) would not be established.
Regarding the successive establishment [of phenomena]:
for a person lacking wisdom, there is no such thing as an untimely death;
rather, all suffering arises from the roots of karma that are nurtured by the results of one's original karma.
From karma arises merit, and from merit arises the Noble Path.
The Path is neither cultivated nor lost.
All other matters are the same as the views of the Mahāsāṃghikas.
Regarding those who hold the fundamental view that "that Caitya, Āpava, Uttara, and Śira [are the ultimate]," the Bodhisattva departs from the evil destinies;
yet, making offerings to a stūpa yields no great fruit.
Arhats possess ignorance regarding the benefit conferred by others and possess doubt;
they attain the Path through the speech of others who observe them.
All other matters are held in common with the Mahāsāṃghikas.
Regarding the fundamental view of the Sarvāstivādins:
they assert that all existing things are comprised of two categories that encompass all phenomena—
namely, name (*nāma*) and form (*rūpa*).
There is a path that extends into future lives;
there is the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) known by the consciousness of phenomena;
and there is the clear understanding of the conditioned characteristics of phenomena—arising, abiding, and ceasing.
Three are unconditioned;
three truths have the characteristic of being conditioned;
one truth has the characteristic of being unconditioned.
The sequential and uninterrupted realization of the Four Truths;
emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
and the transcendence that rises above and leaves birth behind.
Contemplating the transcendence of that which is bound to the desire realm,
one transcends and enters the state of "leaving birth behind" (vairāgya);
fifteen moments of mind constitute the stage of "approaching" (pratipannaka).
The sixteenth moment of mind is called "abiding in the fruit.
The single moment of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) and the preceding three stages of preparation (prayoga) are subject to regression.
The supreme worldly state,
the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna),
is the dharma of non-retrogression.
Arhats possess the quality of falling away from their state.
Not all Arhats attain the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) may attain freedom from desire and ill-will.
The non-Buddhists possess the five supernormal powers;
the various devas also attain the cultivation of the holy life;
and within the seven factors of enlightenment, they attain awakening.
It is not comprised within other dhyānas;
the foundations of mindfulness are attained without depending on dhyāna,
as one transcends and rises above the state of ordinary birth.
One may attain the fruit of arhatship in the realm of form,
yet fail to transcend and depart from the state of birth.
No one among the inhabitants of Uttarakuru attains freedom from desire;
they likewise do not attain the Noble Path.
Furthermore, those in the Heaven of Non-perception do not necessarily attain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya in successive order or leap over stages to transcend birth.
By means of worldly [attainment], one realizes the fruits of Sakṛdāgāmin and Anāgāmin.
Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, all dharmas,
and all latent proclivities associated with the mind— all such latent proclivities [are abandoned].
These are envelopments (paryavasthāna) but not underlying tendencies (anuśaya).
The factors of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda-anga) are conditioned (saṃskṛta).
It is taught that even Arhats possess the factors of dependent origination.
Arhats possess the increase of meritorious qualities.
Within the desire realm and the form realm, there exist the five bodies of consciousness in the intermediate state (antarābhava);
these are the five bodies of consciousness characterized by desire.
It corresponds with itself;
it is neither volition nor a mental factor (caitta). Mind and mental states have their own intrinsic nature as their object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
It is dissociated from its own nature and dissociated from the mind;
yet there exists mundane right view.
There is the mundane faculty of faith;
there is the arhat who is without aspiration;
and there are no dharmas of those in training.
All Arhats attain dhyāna, yet it does not necessarily manifest before them.
Arhats may still experience the retribution of past karma.
There is an unwholesome mind of an ordinary person that undergoes final passing away;
there is no intermediate state of final passing away.
The bodhisattva is an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) who possesses the fetters (saṃyojana),
has not yet transcended or emerged from the state of birth,
and has not yet surpassed the stage of the ordinary person in receiving a body.
The designation of "sentient beings" refers to the total exhaustion and non-existence of all conditioned phenomena;
yet, from this world to another world,
it is spoken of according to worldly convention.
From this world to the next, while life has not yet ended,
all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have been exhausted through grasping;
there is no dharma that undergoes transformation.
There is supramundane dhyāna with vitarka and vicāra that is untainted and wholesome;
this is the cause. Within this meditative concentration, there is no verbal expression.
The Eightfold Noble Path is the Wheel of Dharma.
It is not the case that everything spoken by the Tathāgata constitutes the turning of the wheel of Dharma;
the Buddha does not speak of all matters,
nor does he speak of everything according to its literal meaning.
Not all sūtras are of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*);
there are such intermediate views as these.
As for the fundamental view of the Haimavata school:
Bodhisattvas and ordinary beings alike are free from ignorance;
they purify buddha-fields and descend into their mothers' wombs.
Non-Buddhists do not possess the five supernormal powers;
the various devas are unable to practice the holy life;
and there are arhats who possess ignorance and doubt regarding the benefits conferred by others.
They attain the Path through the speech of others' observations;
all other [views] are identical to the Sarvāstivāda perspective.
Such is the fundamental view of that Vātsīputrīya school.
It is not identical to the person,
nor is it separate from the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases,
because it is a conventional designation based on their combination.
All aggregates do not abide for even a single moment;
apart from the person, there is no dharma that proceeds from this world to another world.
When it is said that a person reaches that [state],
the non-Buddhists possess the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). The five groups of consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*) do not exist there, as they are devoid of desire.

Nor is it the abandonment of desire; rather, one attains the abandonment of desire by severing the fetters and latent tendencies (anuśaya) bound to the realm of desire through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga),
not through the path of seeing the truths (darśanamārga).

Patience (kṣānti) is called the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgra-dharma); transcending and departing from the state of ordinary birth is the arising of the twelve moments of mind, which is termed "approaching" (pratipannaka).
The thirteenth moment of mind is termed "abiding in the fruit" (phalastha).
There are six cities, including Drakṣāvatī, Tilaśayana, and Trimiṭi.
Regarding those who have various other explanations, they may be explained through their respective verses.
Yet they fall once more;
having fallen, they become deeply attached,
obtaining karma from karma.
According to the fundamental view of that Mahīśāsaka school,
there is no past or future;
there is only the present and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Regarding the four noble truths, there is a single direct realization (*abhisamaya*).
Seeing suffering is itself called "seeing";
seeing that which is the truth of suffering is what is meant by "seeing the noble truth."
The various proclivities (anuśaya) are neither mind nor mental factors;
they are not associated with objects.
The proclivities are distinct from the outbursts (paryavasthāna), and the outbursts are likewise distinct from the proclivities.
The fetters dissociated from the mind are associated with the mind.
Ordinary persons do not desire to harbor ill will,
and non-Buddhists lack the five supernormal powers.
The gods cannot practice the holy life;
there is no intermediate state (antarābhava); and Arhats possess no further increase of merit.
The five groups of consciousness are both with desire and free from desire;
the sixth group of consciousness is associated with vitarka and vicāra,
yet lacks mundane right view.
They lack the mundane faculty of faith;
they possess no supramundane dhyāna;
they have no realization of supramundane dharmas.
There is no such thing as being caused by virtue.
There is the possibility of falling away for a stream-enterer (srotāpanna),
and there is also the possibility of falling away for an arhat.
The factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are subsumed under the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
There are nine unconditioned entities (*asaṃskṛtadharma*), namely:
analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), space (*ākāśa*), and the wholesome phenomena (*kuśaladharma*).
Unwholesome phenomena are like indeterminate phenomena;
they are like the dependent origination of the Path;
they are like [the sequence] from the womb up to death.
The sense faculties and the four great elements undergo transformation and perish of their own accord;
the mind and mental factors likewise undergo transformation and perish of their own accord.
Within the Sangha of Buddhas and monks, one may offer gifts to the Sangha.
Attaining great fruits of retribution is not unique to the Buddha;
the Buddha and the śrāvakas are the same in this regard.
They share one path, one liberation, and all their conditioned formations are momentary.
There is no dharma that passes from this world to another world;
such are the fundamental views [of these schools].
These are the various intermediate views.
There exist past and future worlds;
there exists the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the factors of existence (*dharmāyatana*), the cognition of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), and volitional action (*cetanākarma*).
There is no bodily or vocal action associated with applied and sustained thought (*vitarkavicāra*) of the mind.
During the kalpa of dwelling on the great earth,
when the dharma of the minor fruit of retribution for making offerings to a stūpa manifests before one,
it is called the manifestation of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases (*skandha-dhātu-āyatana*).
The seeds of dharmas already existing can give rise to all forms of suffering—
namely, ignorance, craving, views, and karma.
This is called the intermediate vision of dharmas.
According to the fundamental view of that Dharmaguptaka school,
the Buddha cannot be included within the Saṃgha for the purpose of receiving offerings;
the Buddha attains great fruits of retribution and is not part of the Saṃgha.
The Buddha-way differs from the way of the śrāvakas.
Non-Buddhists do not possess the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā).
The body of an arhat is the remainder of that which is free from outflows (anāsrava).
All [these views] are identical to those of the Mahāsāṃghika school.
As for the fundamental view of that Kāśyapīya school:
there is the abandonment of dharmas and the knowledge of their abandonment.
There is no phenomenon that is not subject to cessation which one does not know through the knowledge of cessation.
When karma has ripened, its retribution is experienced;
when it has not ripened, its retribution is not experienced.
There are past causes and effects;
there are no future causes and effects;
all phenomena are momentary.
There are dharmas with vitarka that have retribution;
all other [views] are the same as those of the Dharmaguptaka school.
As for the fundamental views of the Saṃmitīya school:
The aggregates (skandhas) pass from this world to another world;
they cannot be extinguished apart from the Noble Path.
The existence of the aggregates is based upon their fundamental cause.
There is one person whose views are identical to those of the Sarvāstivādins;
this is a brief explanation of the views of all the schools.
The *Śāstra on the Eighteen Schools*, one fascicle: This treatise was erroneously duplicated within the Song edition of the Tripiṭaka.
Since the work concerning the divergent tenets of those schools is titled the *Śāstra on the Eighteen Schools*, I have now adopted this national edition as the correct version.
The *Kaiyuan lu* states: "Regarding these eighteen treatises on the right, various catalogs all claim they were translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha during the Liang dynasty.
Now, upon careful examination, it appears that the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha has already translated eighteen treatises."
It is not appropriate to translate this again as a treatise on the differing tenets of the schools.
At the beginning of this treatise on the eighteen schools, it cites the "Section on Differentiation" from the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*;
subsequently, it states that it was compiled by the Dharma Master Kumārajīva, and only after that does the main body of the treatise follow.
If this were translated by Kumārajīva,
it would be inconsistent for him to cite the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchāsūtra*— which did not yet exist during the Qin period— and place it at the beginning.
Alternatively, it may be appropriate to classify the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* as a work of lost translation according to the *Bié lù*.
There is no doubt that this [text] was cited during the Qin period.
If it were a re-translation by Paramārtha, [it would have been included in his catalog].
In the commentary on the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, the inclusion of the character "Qin" (秦) is inappropriate.
Upon examining its literary style and structure, it is largely a translation produced by Kumārajīva during the Qin period.
It is likely that various catalogs omitted this section from their compendia, which has led to these doubts.

Regarding the commentaries on the eighteen schools of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, namely the *Bhinnasamaya-viniścaya-śāstra*: although this principle exists, I did not venture to point it out previously.
